articles.title: “Karl Saw That Her Potential Isn’t Only In The Paint” – WNBA Fans Erupt As Angel Reese Hones 3-Pt Shot Amid Shooting Breakthrough
articles.summary: Angel Reese has been nothing short of legendary in the 2026 WNBA Finals, as the Atlanta Dream leads the series 2-1. The Golden State Valkyries were the best...
articles.body:
Angel Reese has been nothing short of legendary in the 2026 WNBA Finals, as the Atlanta Dream leads the series 2-1. The Golden State Valkyries were the best defensive team this season, led by talented players like Gabby Williams. However, Reese has overpowered everyone so far, and her practice routine has now taken the internet by storm.

Reese led the team to a Game 3 win in Atlanta in front of the home crowd, scoring 21 points and grabbing 12 rebounds in 34 minutes. Moreover, her 3-point shooting, which drew heavy criticism during the regular season, has improved. She shot 2-for-2 from deep and garnered praise from veterans.

Meanwhile, the Dream player was seen practicing her long-range shots before Game 4 of the WNBA Finals.

Meanwhile, fans were impressed with Reese's workout, as one pointed out Dream head coach Karl Smesko's impact on her form:

"I'm so happy Karl saw that her potential isn't only in the paint🥹," one fan wrote.

Reese is averaging 21.7 points, 13.3 rebounds, 2.0 assists, 2.0 steals, and 1.0 block per game in the final series. Her impact on both ends of the floor has been great, and she has put forward a strong case for the Finals MVP title.

Angel Reese reveals her mental game against the Valkyries

Angel Reese is one of the most intense players on the court, often through trash talk and mind games. The Finals have also featured intense, competitive moments involving the 2026 Defensive Player of the Year.

In a conversation with the media, Reese shared her secret to success in the ongoing series:

"You can see it in their emotions and facial expressions. A lot of us are looking at that, making sure we can find any little thing to give us that edge and have our leverage over them."

Angel Reese and the Dream are in a strong spot in the series and just a couple of games away from the title. Game 4 tips off Saturday as fans await who picks up the championship this season.

articles.title: Brewers hold on for 3-2 win over Rays in Game 1
articles.summary: It isn’t often that we are treated to a World Series matchup featuring the two best teams in the league. The Brewers won an NL-best 103 games during the regu...
articles.body:
It isn't often that we are treated to a World Series matchup featuring the two best teams in the league. The Brewers won an NL-best 103 games during the regular season while the Rays paced the AL with 98. The matchup lived up to its billing in Game 1 with a thrilling finish.

Milwaukee carried a 3-1 lead into the ninth with closer Trevor Megill on the mound. Milwaukee's relievers entered the series with a 1.33 ERA in 40 2/3 postseason innings. Megill got Yandy Diaz to ground out to start the frame but then allowed back-to-back singles to Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson. With Junior Caminero representing the go-ahead run at the plate, the Rays stayed aggressive and pulled off a double steal to put the tying runs into scoring position.

Megill walked Caminero to load the bases to bring up Liam Hicks and that is when things got interesting. Hicks grounded the first pitch he saw into what appeared to be a game-ending double play. However, the Rays challenged and the replay showed that shortstop Cooper Pratt's foot was off the bag at second when he received the throw from Brice Turang.

Pinch runner Jorge Mateo scored on the play to cut the lead to 3-2. Having thought the game was over, Megill had to come back out with the tying run at third but struck out Jonny DeLuca with a nasty curveball to seal the win.

Catcher William Contreras played a big part in the win for the Brewers. He followed Christian Yelich's RBI triple with a 108 mph single off of shortstop Taylor Walls' glove to stake the Brewers to a 2-0 lead in the first inning.

He also had an impact behind the plate. With the Brewers leading 2-1 in the fifth, Contreras gunned down Victor Mesa Jr. who was trying to steal third with a perfect throw to end the inning.

He also threw out Aranda in the sixth on a failed hit-and-run attempt that ended another threat. Contreras finished the game with two hits, a walk and was also successful on two ABS challenges rounding out an all-around effort.

Jacob Misiorowski got the start for the Brewers on the mound and needed just one pitch to set a World Series record. His 103.5 mph fastball to Diaz to start the game was the fastest recorded pitch in World Series history dating back to 2008 when pitch tracking began.

It wasn't Misiorowski's sharpest performance, but he did what he needed to do to keep the Brewers in front. He worked out of a jam in the first inning where Aranda and Chandler Simpson reached with back-to-back singles. However, Misiorowski got Caminero to line into a double play to end the inning. He allowed a single run in the fourth and exited after the fifth having allowed four hits to go along with three strikeouts.

The Brewers added an insurance run in the seventh on a run-scoring single by Jackson Chourio that pushed the lead to 3-1. Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby combined for three scoreless innings in relief before turning things over to Megill in the ninth. Ashby has been one of the best pitchers in the postseason running his streak to 14 scoreless innings across seven appearances.

The two teams will meet again on Saturday for Game 2 of the series. Logan Henderson will get the start for Milwaukee while Tampa will go with righty ace Drew Rasmussen.

articles.title: Brewers Hold Off Rays in Game 1 Thriller to Take World Series Lead
articles.summary: Yelich Gives Milwaukee an Early Spark The Brewers wasted little time getting on the scoreboard. Christian Yelich delivered an RBI triple in the bottom of the...
articles.body:
The Brewers wasted little time getting on the scoreboard. Christian Yelich delivered an RBI triple in the bottom of the first inning to give Milwaukee a 1-0 lead. William Contreras followed with an RBI single, extending the advantage to 2-0 and immediately putting pressure on Tampa Bay's pitching staff.

On the mound, rookie right-hander Jacob Misiorowski made an impression early. He fired a 103.5 mph pitch, setting a World Series velocity record in the pitch-tracking era. His electric fastball gave Milwaukee a major weapon as the Brewers attempted to keep Tampa Bay's lineup under control.

The Rays finally broke through in the fourth inning when Liam Hicks grounded out to bring home a run, cutting the deficit to 2-1. Tampa Bay continued looking for opportunities, but Milwaukee's pitching and defense limited the damage.

Milwaukee regained a two run cushion in the seventh inning. Jackson Chourio delivered an RBI single to make it 3-1, giving the Brewers a valuable insurance run heading into the final innings.

The hit proved crucial as Tampa Bay continued battling. The Rays threatened in the ninth, cutting the deficit to one run when Liam Hicks brought home a runner. Tampa Bay also attempted a double steal to put the tying run in scoring position, creating a tense situation for Milwaukee's bullpen.

However, the Brewers managed to escape the late threat and secure the final out, protecting the narrow lead and sending the home crowd into celebration.

The 3-2 victory gives Milwaukee a 1-0 lead in the World Series and provides an important confidence boost after a long postseason journey. The Brewers received contributions from their offense early, added a key insurance run late and held on when the Rays made their final push.

Yelich and Contreras set the tone in the opening inning, while Chourio's seventh-inning hit ultimately helped make the difference.

Milwaukee will now look to carry that momentum into Game 2. With the opening victory secured, the Brewers have an opportunity to put additional pressure on Tampa Bay and move one step closer to the franchise's first World Series championship.

articles.title: 3 adjustments Valkyries must make to bounce back in WNBA Finals Game 4 vs. Dream
articles.summary: ATLANTA – The Golden State Valkyries are itching to get back onto the court and under the spotlight, down 2-1 heading into Game 4 of the WNBA Finals. The ang...
articles.body:
ATLANTA – The Golden State Valkyries are itching to get back onto the court and under the spotlight, down 2-1 heading into Game 4 of the WNBA Finals . The angst, the emotion, the frustration, the fight– the Valkyries are dying to unleash it all and exorcise their demons from their ugly 97-71 Game 3 loss to the Atlanta Dream.

"We're hungry," Valkyries forward Kaila Charles said at the team's Friday afternoon practice. "This has been the longest two days ever. I'm ready to play again. But I think our spirits are really high. We understand what we need to do, and we're excited to get another chance."

Game 4 is a chance Golden State doesn't take lightly, a window of opportunity that can and will close in an instant. Either they tie the series up heading back to their raucous home crowd in Ballhalla, or they find themselves in the quicksand of a 3-1 deficit and on the brink of their magic run to the Finals dissipating into dust.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

As such, the Valkyries require making some major adjustments to stifle the Dream, who've set the tone the entire series thus far. From Angel Reese steamrolling them to the cup and giving them the "petite" gesture, along the way to Atlanta as a whole squeezing the life out of the Golden State offense and forcing them into uncharacteristic turnovers, it's adapt or go extinct for the Valkyries at this juncture of the series.

So here are three aspects of the series the Valkyries need to address and adjust to even things up at 2-2 and get back to their brand of unrelenting, strength-in-numbers basketball.

The Valkyries must uncork the halfcourt offense

It's not surprising that Golden State's been rendered completely ineffective in the halfcourt this series. After all, the Dream boast the Defensive Player of the Year and have the length and athleticism to blunt a lot of what the Valkyries like to do best, specifically their drive-and-kick, stampede actions – where a player catches the ball on the run as they cut after the initiator draws the defense.

Nor has it been a surprise when it seems like every single shot Golden State attempts has a hand in their face or a Dream defender all the way in their airspace– the Valkyries boasted one of the toughest shot difficulties all season long, with their best shotmakers having some of the lower expected field goal percentages in the league.

But it has been a decisive factor in the tenor of this series. Atlanta has completely taken away Golden State's transition opportunities, the part of the game where their offense is cleanest and when the Valkyries can unload the avalanche on teams, making their halfcourt execution even more important. So far this series, they haven't come close to cracking the Dream's shell defense, designed to gap their drives and force them into 1-on-1 iso basketball.

So the Valkyries know what they need to do: score more points in the halfcourt. Obviously. But how they do that is the real conundrum.

Because while Gabby Williams has risen to a star-level talent these playoffs, her on-ball will just never draw two defenders to her in the way a truly A1 offensive talent demands, which is not a knock on her, just a statement of fact for how Atlanta has defended her this series. And while it's easy to say "scrap the scheme" when the scheme isn't working, you can't just do that in the middle of a Finals series; you don't have time.

So at this juncture, Golden State is going to have to lean on their strength-in-numbers philosophy to solve the Dream's defense. That could mean leaning more into the depth that has done well offensively this series. Tiffany Hayes seems like the one Valkyrie who can consistently punch the paint. Janelle Salaun came alive in Game 3; at her best, she can overcome a hand in her face and bury any-and-all catch-and-shoot triples.

From Williams' point of view, it comes down to being more decisive, which melds into coach Natalie Nakase's point about cutting down on turnovers. Overall, the Valkyries have been controlling the tempo, reducing possessions, and getting extra possessions from steals and offensive rebounds. Those are key factors that can certainly help loosen up their offensive slog. But the fact of the matter is they'll just need to make some tough buckets. A simple solution, but hard to make a reality with the way Atlanta's defending.

The Valkyries must slow down Angel Reese

On the flip side, and a far more controllable variable than their high-variance offense, is the Valkyries' defense, which still hasn't solved Reese, despite that side of the court being the defining trait of their run to the Finals.

It's not for a lack of effort. Golden State has used center Kiah Stokes with some success, but it comes at the cost of clogging their offense's spacing. And when Stokes hasn't been on the floor, Reese has literally burned everyone else. Aminata Gueye? Torched – and trash-talked along the way. Kayla Thornton? Not big enough and not quick enough. Salaun? Hasn't been fast enough laterally for the quick Reese. Laeticia Amihere? Outmuscled whenever she doesn't have a help defender behind her to deter Reese.

So what's the adjustment? Well, it's not as simple as showing two at Reese or loading up the help behind her like they did to A'ja Wilson in the Las Vegas Aces series.

For one, the Dream are doing a great job putting her in spots that make it terrible tactically to do either of those things, unless you are comfortable with any one of her four teammates getting a wide-open shot, something Wilson didn't really have the luxury of. And for another, it may just be better to let Reese get hers and keep every other Dream player locked up and out of rhythm. The Valkyries' defense got completely worked when Reese started getting everyone else involved. Whether it was her leading the break or finding the right pass when all eyes were on her, she's deadliest when she's bullying the Valkyries enough to send even more resources at her.

That doesn't mean don't guard her. Nakase should probably be matching Stokes minutes with her at this point – and find a way to make her more useful offensively – and Amihere has a case for getting more run against her. Maybe even throw Kaila Charles at her. She's had the most fight and energy of any Valkyrie these Finals, as she didn't back down when she and Rhyne Howard got into it. It also helps that she played with Reese in AAU on Team Takeover in Maryland; she might intuitively remember some age-old secrets to defending her.

But ultimately, Golden State needs to limit her on the offensive boards; she has 11 in the Finals and had five in Game 3. Again, easier said than done against the best rebounder in the league. But those kinds of plays become back-breaking over the course of a game, and if they want to win the possession battle, it behooves the Valkyries to consider boxing her out with even more attention.

The Valkyries must find the fire and get back to Golden State basketball

But X's and O's and tactics aside, the Valkyries believe their shortcomings in Games 2 and 3 all stem from not playing like themselves. And wrapped into that is the way Reese and the Dream have won the mind game battle in how she's fired herself up with the trash talk. Those kinds of things give Atlanta their edge – their motivation. The Valkyries have motivation; it just hasn't translated into their hoops. And they know it .

"We need to have some fire, too," Charles said when asked about how Reese has gone at Gueye specifically and how the Valkyries as a whole deal with those kinds of interactions. "People (don't) necessarily (have to be) trash talkers, but being more physical, imposing our will, and dictating the game that way."

Charles' answer underscores Golden State's most needed adjustment– get back to playing Valkyries basketball and get back to setting the tone. The Dream have taken them away from their identity better than any team has this season. But what makes a team great– what makes a team worthy of a championship– is being unshakable. And being unshakable means finding a way, no matter the circumstances, something the Valkyries have done all season long.

"There's been moments in games this season where it feels like there's no way we're gonna win this," Veronica Burton said. "And you could say that there's no way the Valkyries are gonna be here, whatever it may be. And you find a way, and you will it out, and you do it together, and you grind it out. That's what has allowed us to get here. That's what allowed us to beat LA, or what allowed us to beat Dallas in Game 3 when we're down (16). Like, logistically, it doesn't make much sense, but you come together, and you find a way to do it, and that's what it comes down to."

The heart of a champion rests inside the Valkyries. We've all heard it beat loudly whenever they've defied the odds and upended our expectations. So maybe the biggest adjustment they can make in Game 4 is to revive that pulse. Because if we've learned anything this season, if Burton and her squad have a pulse, they have a fighting chance.

articles.title: Que no te engañen. La silla gaming Soma Chroma es más que luces: es comodidad de alto nivel
articles.summary: Sobre el papel, la Razer Soma Chroma es una de esas sillas gaming que corren el riesgo de parecer más un capricho que otra cosa, puesto que la primera impresión que ofrece es la de una silla muy llamativa que destaca por su iluminación RGB.
articles.body: Sobre el papel, la Razer Soma Chroma es una de esas sillas gaming que corren el riesgo de parecer más un capricho que otra cosa, puesto que la primera impresión que ofrece es la de una silla muy llamativa que destaca por su iluminación RGB. No obstante, esta primera impresión no debe engañarte, puesto que detrás de todo ese muy bonito sistema de iluminación se esconde una silla bastante top que destaca, entre otras cosas, por su ergonomía. Para entenderlo tuve que probarla durante un tiempo, y fue esto lo que me convenció de que su propuesta iba más allá de una silla con luces de una marca a la que ya conocemos. Porque sí, la iluminación RGB es uno de sus factores más destacados. Es lo que, entre otras cosas, le da personalidad, pero lo que realmente importa es que es una silla cómoda, elegante, resistente y muy práctica. Me sorprendió, la verdad. Razer se podría haber conformado con ofrecer un diseño llamativo que justificase su precio, pero decidió ir más allá. Siendo sincero, me alegro de que haya sido de esta manera, porque para mí lo más importante en una silla es que sea cómoda. La ergonomía y la salud de la espalda son los elementos que más importancia deben tener en cualquier producto de estas características y en este caso estamos ante una que cumple con buena nota en ambos. Bien pertrechada con acabados de calidad y un sistema de montaje mucho más sencillo de lo que parece, el resultado final es el de un producto que mezcla ese capricho de iluminación con esa necesidad de estar sentado en una buena silla. Así pues, lo primero que os puedo decir es que estar sentado en ella se siente muy bien. La Soma Chroma viene equipada con espuma de doble densidad curada en frío. En otras palabras, es un sistema que tiene por objetivo ofrecer una sensación mullida mientras se reparte la presión al estar sentado. Si lo traduzco a la práctica, el sentimiento es agradable. Es cómoda. Además, los reposabrazos también están acolchados, por lo que la idea de pasar varias horas sentado frente al ordenador en ella no es un problema. Es más, lo hice y no me sentí pesado en ningún momento. Tanto es así que, a título personal, me parece una de las sillas más cómodas de Razer. No porque el asiento sea blando, ya que no lo es en exceso, sino porque la sensación general es buena. La postura básica es sólida y no resulta incómoda. En ese sentido, ayuda mucho que su respaldo se pueda reclinar hasta 155 grados, lo cual no está nada mal. Cierto es que no es la silla más destacada en ese sentido, y que tampoco está pensada para ello, pero ahí está. Si tuviese que ponerle alguna pega, es que quizá le habría sentado bien la capacidad de ajustar más tanto este aspecto como el resto de condicionantes a la hora de estar sentado. Por ejemplo, el soporte lumbar no se puede ajustar en posición o intensidad, y aunque tiene una curvatura integrada muy agradable, la posibilidad de ajustarlo siempre es un extra. Sucede lo mismo con los reposabrazos, que solo disponen de regulación de altura y lateral. Pese a ello, no considero que sea una mala silla. Más bien todo lo contrario. Es realmente cómoda, por lo que estos detalles son más bien aspectos que podrían mejorar, pero que no devalúan el resultado final. Es muy buena silla. Luego está el tema de la iluminación. Si quieres darle un toque extra a tu setup y que sea más resultón, lo cierto es que la Soma Chroma puede ser justo lo que estés buscando. El acabado con silueta deportiva en negro y detalles verdes con iluminación RGB la convierten en una de las sillas más espectaculares del mercado en términos visuales. Es perfecta para streaming y grabación. Pero su acabado gaming no la hace menos elegante. No es un conjunto de colores resultones sin más, sino que mantiene la sobriedad propia que le pedimos a una marca como Razer. Tomando en consideración todos estos aspectos, y con un precio recomendado de 529,99 euros, la Soma Chroma es una gran silla. Hay que entender que se trata de un producto premium, por lo que lo más importante es considerar si es lo que buscas o no. Razer tiene un abanico muy amplio de opciones y esta, posiblemente, esté más pensada para los que buscan darle a su setup un toque extra para que sus grabaciones, streamings, etc., sean incluso más llamativos. Pese a ello, no debemos pensar que se orienta solo a este aspecto, porque el acabado es muy bueno y la ergonomía es de alto nivel. Cumple en ambos ámbitos con buena nota. En definitiva, la Razer Soma Chroma es mucho más que colores. Es una silla elegante, resistente, práctica y, sobre todo, muy cómoda. Las luces son la carta de presentación, pero es el conjunto lo que hace que termine convenciendo.
